llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan  
“Infrequent Payment Schemes and the Financial & Productivity Outcomes of Kenyan Tea Farmers”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-------------------------------------------------
Preferred: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event–study extension.  

Why appropriate  
• Balanced panel of farmers observed several years before and after the policy.  
• Clear treatment start date (introduction of the infrequent-payment option).  
• Rich administrative data allow farmer fixed effects and time fixed effects, removing all time-invariant heterogeneity and common shocks.  
• An event-study (dynamic DID) will document pre-trends and the evolution of effects.  

Optional refinement (addressing self-selection)  
Use a two-stage DID-IV in which “eligibility for the infrequent scheme” (defined by an institutional threshold—e.g., minimum average monthly deliveries in the prior year) instruments for actual take-up. This is a fuzzy DID-RD hybrid but can be implemented with a standard 2SLS in panel form.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition  
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 if farmer i is on the infrequent-payment contract in year/quarter t; 0 otherwise.  

Control group  
Farmers who remain on the regular (monthly) payment schedule throughout. They provide the counterfactual change in outcomes absent the new payment scheme.  

Treatment timing  
POST_t = 1 for all observations in periods t ≥ t₀, where t₀ is the season/year the firm officially introduced the option (e.g., July 2017).  

Difference-in-Differences indicator  
DID_it = TREAT_i × POST_t. (If adoption is staggered, set POST varying by individual first-adoption date and estimate a staggered DID with the Callaway-Sant’Anna or Sun-Abraham estimator.)

Running variable / cutoff (if IV used)  
RUN_i = Average kg of green-leaf delivered in the 12 months before t₀.  
Eligibility_i = 1{RUN_i ≥ C}, where C is the administratively announced cutoff (e.g., 3,000 kg).  
Eligibility is predetermined and strongly predicts take-up; it therefore serves as an instrument.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of treatment, outcomes of treated and control farmers would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Farmers sell to the same factory, face identical prices and weather; testing with pre-period trends is feasible.

A2. No Anticipation: Farmers could not perfectly adjust behavior before knowing the scheme details (announcement was close to rollout).  
Plausibility: Institutional accounts suggest a short announcement window.

A3. SUTVA / No Spillovers: A farmer’s payment frequency does not alter neighbors’ outcomes (e.g., local input markets are not capacity-constrained).  
Plausibility: Some risk of peer borrowing spillovers; we will test for spatial spillovers using GIS distance to treated farms.

A4. Stable Composition: Entry/exit of farmers is unrelated to treatment status after conditioning on FE.  
Plausibility: Attrition in tea farming is low; we will show balanced panels and conduct Lee-bounds.

A5. First-stage relevance & exclusion (IV only): Eligibility strongly predicts take-up and affects outcomes only through payment frequency.  
Plausibility: The cutoff was designed solely for administrative simplicity, not for differential assistance.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
-------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Self-selection into the scheme (more disciplined farmers opt in).  
Fix: (i) Event-study pre-trend test; (ii) DID-IV using exogenous eligibility; (iii) control for baseline savings, yields, and farmer fixed effects.

Threat 2: Differential shocks (e.g., localized pests, weather, COVID) coinciding with treatment.  
Fix: Include factory-month or sub-county-month fixed effects; interact rainfall and shock dummies with treatment status; cluster SEs at factory × year level.

Threat 3: Spillover/General-equilibrium effects (credit or labor markets).  
Fix: Add controls for cooperative-level credit supply; estimate spatial spillovers within 2 km bands; show robustness excluding high-density clusters.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # panel regressions
library(did)             # Callaway–Sant’Anna event study
library(modelsummary)    # nice tables

# 1. Load Data -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("tea_farmers_raw.csv")   # one row per farmer-year-quarter

# 2. Variable Construction ----------------------------------------------
# Policy introduction date
policy_start <- as.Date("2017-07-01")

dt[, post        := date >= policy_start]
dt[, treat       := (payment_scheme == "infrequent")]
dt[, did         := treat * post]

# Outcomes
dt[, log_yield   := log(1 + kg_greenleaf)]
dt[, savings     := savings_balance]
dt[, invest_capx := input_expenditure]

# Eligibility instrument (optional IV)
cutoff <- 3000
dt[, run_var     := pre_policy_12m_kg]
dt[, eligible    := (run_var >= cutoff)]

# Fixed effects identifiers
dt[, yearq       := paste0(year(date), "Q", quarter(date))]

# 3. Main DID Specification ---------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(log_yield ~ did | id + yearq, data = dt, se = "cluster=id")
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study (pre-trends) -------------------------------------------
es <- feols(log_yield ~ sunab(first_treat, yearq) | id + yearq,
            data = dt, se = "cluster=id")
iplot(es)                 # event-study graph

# 5. DID-IV Specification -----------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(log_yield ~ 1 | id + yearq | treat ~ eligible,
                 data = dt, se = "cluster=id")
summary(iv_main)

# 6. Robustness: Farmer-specific linear trends --------------------------
dt[, trend := as.numeric(as.yearmon(date))]   # monthly numeric
did_trend <- feols(log_yield ~ did + i(trend, id) | id + yearq,
                   data = dt, se = "cluster=id")
summary(did_trend)

# 7. Export Table --------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(DID = did_main, EventStudy = es, DID_IV = iv_main,
                  DID_Trends = did_trend),
             stars = TRUE, output = "results_table.docx")
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: Larger, lump-sum payments operate as a commitment device that (i) reduce “temptation” spending, (ii) relax lump-sum liquidity constraints for lumpy input purchases, and (iii) possibly improve bargaining within the household.  
Prior:  
• Tea yield ↑ ≈ 5–8 %.  
• Savings balances ↑ ≈ 15–25 %.  
• Input investment ↑ ≈ 10 %.  
We expect negligible effects on short-term consumption but higher end-of-season profits.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends checked and flat ………………… 1  
C2 No contemporaneous confounders (time FE, shocks)… 1  
C3 Stable treatment and control composition …………… 0.5  
C4 No spillovers/SUTVA ……………………………………… 0.5  
C5 Correct standard-error clustering …………………… 1  

Total = 4/5.
